replication.target_description: Comparison of feminine-masculine word pairs and masculine generics on the number of women named. Target correspondence unresolved unless explicitly stated in notes.

notes: Identity independently checked: title matches Effects of the Generic Masculine and its Alternatives in Germanophone countries; title-page authors begin Hilmar Brohmer and Gabriela Hofer and include the named collaboration, Sczesny, Stahlberg and Athenstaedt. Header Source URL https://osf.io/q56rk/download agrees with the q56rk identifier in the neutral DOI reference. This is an accepted CONFIRMATORY REPORT with final-data Results and Discussion, not a preregistration or abstract-only parse. DOI is not separately printed in the body. Canonical text includes pages 0–44, but Tables 1 and 2 and figures are not text-recovered. No PDF supplied; no rendering possible. Locator pagination differs from this accepted version: p.14 is procedure, p.12 is power planning; substantive final results are pp.21–25. Only unfinished_fields were assessed; original and other unassigned fields are null placeholders. The named comparison occurs in both the four-category close replication and the six-category extension. The p.14 locator is procedure in this source version and does not distinguish the tests. H1 candidates: internal-I vs generic masculine t(1475)=21.09, d=1.37; feminine-masculine vs generic masculine t(1475)=8.15, d=0.51; each p < .001. H2 Table 4 candidates: GM vs II z-Ratio=-23.01, ratio=0.49; GM vs FM z-Ratio=-11.04, ratio=0.71; each Bonferroni p < .001. Requested metric is test statistic; retain t and z as distinct printed candidates, with no conversion or selection. Both H1 and H2 narrative findings favor feminine-masculine over generic masculine, but the stale page locator does not identify the intended sample/test; a positive verdict is retained as candidate evidence only.
